title: 'I Play Rocky' revives the gamble that made Sylvester Stallone a superstar
summary: The "I Play Rocky" trailer reveals how Sylvester Stallone refused massive paydays to star in his own screenplay, a gamble experts call unheard of.
story: The actor explained that his relationship with Stallone started off as professional since Stallone was his boss, but they developed a friendship.

Sylvester Stallone's historic "Rocky" story will be retold in Peter Farrelly's biographical drama, "I Play Rocky." To bring it to life, Farrelly had to flash back to how "Rocky" became a household name, and it started with Stallone selling his screenplay only if he was cast as the lead role.

In the "I Play Rocky" trailer, Stallone, played by Anthony Ippolito, presents the script that he wrote in three days to movie producers. They offered him outrageous amounts of money for the script, but Stallone wouldn't budge. Eventually, the producers gave in and cast Stallone in the role that changed his life.
Experts told Fox News Digital this move from Stallone was highly unheard of at the time.
Sylvester Stallone wrote "Rocky" in three days and refused to sell his screenplay unless he was cast as the lead role. (Getty Images)
"It was unheard of at the time, especially for someone in Stallone's economic situation, which was dire," film historian Dwight Cleveland said.
In the trailer, Stallone worked as a valet attendant when he created "Rocky."
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS GRUELING ‘ROCKY’ PREP: ‘IF YOU WANT IT TO FEEL REAL, YOU HAVE TO LIVE IT’

Tisha Morris, entertainment attorney at Legacy Arts Law, said, "Stallone’s decision was extraordinarily unusual. Most first-time writers would have been expected to take the money and relinquish casting control."
From a legal standpoint, Stallone had every right to pull the move he did.

"Legally, Stallone could retain the screenplay and impose that condition because he owned the copyright," she continued. "However, the risk was whether the producers would simply walk away, leaving him with neither a sale nor a film. He was effectively betting the screenplay’s entire market value on himself as an actor."
Cleveland said Stallone acted just like his character in the movies when it came to the initial negotiations.

"Just like his character, Stallone had the confidence his story was a true winner, so he held his ground knowing that this was his shot at stardom both as an actor and as an author," he said. "He wasn't willing to give that up to someone else and be left without any clout in Hollywood. Film depicts the human condition and, in this case, it was true to the heart."
Talia Shire and Sylvester Stallone appear on a poster for "Rocky" in 1976. (Getty Images)

Marc Simon, entertainment attorney at Fox Rothschild in New York, told Fox News Digital Stallone's unwillingness to budge is one of the most-cited examples in Hollywood history of an unknown talent turning down life-changing money on principle.

"Stallone was an unknown actor with only minor bit parts to his name, and producers Robert Chartoff and Irwin Winkler wanted to buy his script outright — with reports indicating the offers escalated to $360,000 with stars (such as Ryan O'Neal, Burt Reynolds and James Caan) identified for the lead role," Simon said.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"In monetary terms today, it’s probably the equivalent of someone being offered over $2 million. Stallone bet everything on starring in the film — a role that no one wanted him to play. He owned the property, and put it all on the line for his million-to-one shot, and like Rocky himself left an indelible mark on cinema and culture, which will be an everlasting legacy."
Beatrice Straight and Sylvester Stallone at the 49th Academy Awards in 1977. (Getty Images)
According to Simon, it was a win-win for producers to ultimately agree to Stallone's terms.

"Financially, Stallone's insistence on starring came paired with his willingness to accept a dramatically reduced salary and rights fee, which lowered the film's overall budget risk at a time when 'Rocky' was made on a modest budget of roughly $1 million," he said. "So, the economics became more palatable to a studio like United Artists that was otherwise wary of an unknown actor carrying the film."

Released in 1976, "Rocky" became one of the biggest underdog success stories in Hollywood history. The movie follows small-time Philadelphia boxer Rocky Balboa as he gets the once-in-a-lifetime chance to fight heavyweight champion Apollo Creed.
Sylvester Stallone on the set of his movie "Rocky II." (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Made on a modest budget, Rocky was both a critical and commercial hit, earning 10 Academy Award nominations (including Best Actor and Best Original Screenplay for Stallone) and winning three Oscars for Best Picture, Best Director for John G. Avildsen and Best Film Editing.
"Rocky" went on to launch one of cinema's most successful franchises and cemented Rocky Balboa as one of the most iconic characters in movie history.
Sylvester Stallone became a household name thanks to the "Rocky" franchise. (Getty Images)

Amazon is gearing up to release "I Play Rocky" in November. According to reports, Stallone is not involved in the biopic. Speaking to The Playlist, Stallone said, "I was shocked to read [about] it. I have zero to do with it."
Ippolito will star as Stallone, and AnnaSophia Robb will play Sasha Czack, Stallone's first wife. Other members of the cast include: Stephan James, Matt Dillon and P.J. Byrne.

title: 'Baywatch: Hawaii' star Brandy Ledford says she 'wanted to truly check out' before rehab saved her life
summary: Brandy Ledford shares how substance abuse nearly destroyed her before rehab and why connecting with fans on Passes is part of her journey in building close connections.
story: The actress, now a wellness advocate and content creator at Passes, shares how trusting God, connecting with her ‘sober sisters’ and telling her story changed her life after rehab.
Brandy Ledford has plenty of reasons to celebrate these days.
The actress, who made hearts race as lifeguard Dawn Masterton on "Baywatch: Hawaii," recently marked 14 years of sobriety.
Today, the 57-year-old is a wellness advocate, yoga teacher and creator on Passes, where she shares exclusive content and connects directly with fans.
But before she found peace, Ledford said she reached her breaking point.
CARA DELEVINGNE ADMITS SHE USED PARTY DRUG GHB DAILY BEFORE TERRIFYING SEIZURES FORCED HER SOBER
"Baywatch: Hawaii" alum Brandy Ledford, now a content creator on Passes, spoke to Fox News Digital about her sobriety journey. (Caroline Malouf)

"There was a moment when I realized something had to change in my life," Ledford told Fox News Digital. "I definitely was abusing substances to avoid my feelings. And I was doing it in a way that was really harmful to me, to my mental health and to my family. And I had a harrowing last night before I checked myself into rehab.
"I didn't know there was going to be a way out."
Brandy Ledford is seen here as Dawn Masterton in "Baywatch: Hawaii." (ZUMA Press Inc./ALAMY)
Ledford said addiction ultimately left her feeling trapped, hopeless and convinced nothing could numb her pain.
WATCH: ‘BAYWATCH’ STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS FAITH HELPED TRANSFORM HER SOBRIETY JOURNEY

"I didn't feel like there was a way out," she shared. "Drinking didn't solve my problems. I was addicted to prescription pain medication. [That] didn't solve my problems. And, in the end, it didn't really take away any of the things I didn't want to be feeling. And that was my last hope. And when I figured that that didn't work anymore, I really just wanted to truly check out because I didn't see a way out."
Brandy Ledford starred in the 2000 television series "Andromeda" opposite Kevin Sorbo. (Fireworks Entertainment/Album/Alamy)

Ledford previously told Basic magazine she struggled with alcohol and drug addiction for much of her life. According to the outlet, she began smoking marijuana at age 11 and was using cocaine and drinking alcohol by age 14. Ledford was jailed twice on alcohol-related charges before turning 17 and developed a cocaine addiction by 18.
Years later, Ledford said she reached a turning point after what she described as "a really horrible last night," the moment she realized something had to change.
Brandy Ledford attends the Silver Spoon Beauty Buffet sponsored by Allure on Day 1 in 2003. (WireImage for Silver Spoon (formerly The Cabana))
"The next day, I checked myself into rehab and found the way out," she said.
Ledford said the greatest gift sobriety gave her wasn't the one she expected. Instead, she found something she never knew she was missing.
Brandy Ledford attends the 6th Jam For Janie Grammy Awards Viewing Party presented by Live Nation at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles Feb. 2, 2025. (Getty Images for Janie's Fund)

"The friendships," she said, fighting back tears. "I didn’t know that I would find my best friends in sobriety. I have a really solid network of girlfriends I've had for 40 years, and they’re here in my life. I made a couple of friends in sobriety who are my lifelines.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Hilary Roberts (left) and Brandy Ledford arrive at the 33rd Annual Race To Erase MS Gala at Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles June 5, 2026. (Steve Granitz/FilmMagic)

"I didn't expect the friendships," she said. "I didn't know that was a possibility. Then I found the community and the network of sober sisters who really support each other and lift each other through everything we go through. I didn't expect my life would be perfect. I never thought, 'Oh good, now I'm sober, everything's going to line up.' But I do know that if I stay sober, eventually things line up. And I learned that from the really brave women in this recovery program."
Brandy Ledford's movie debut came with a memorable role in "Demolition Man" alongside Sylvester Stallone. (JC Olivera/Getty Images)
Ledford once kept her addiction struggles private. Today, she's sharing her story in hopes of inspiring others to seek recovery while leaning on her faith in God every step of the way.
The actress said sharing her recovery journey has become one of the most meaningful parts of her life.

Friendly House Board member Brandy Ledford speaks onstage during Friendly House's 33rd Annual Awards Luncheon at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills, on Oct. 28, 2023. (Getty Images for Friendly House)

"It really is one day at a time," she said. "I give a lot of credit to my higher power, my God, because I couldn't do it without God's help. I have a strong faith. I also didn't expect people to want to hear from somebody in the public about their sobriety. I didn't expect so many people to talk to me about my sobriety and be helped by my story. And what I love about that is I'm able to share my experience so that my experience wasn't wasted.

"I went through a lot, a lot of really challenging, tough times," she said. "And the fact that I can use that now to help others and create strength and hope in others — and in myself — is such a gift of sobriety. It's such a way to keep us sober, to share our stories. But I never really expected people wanted to hear what I had to say.
Brandy Ledford and Carmen Electra attend the 33rd Annual Race To Erase MS Gala at Fairmont Century Plaza in Los Angeles June 5, 2026. (Getty Images for Race to Erase MS)

"I didn't expect to ever talk about that in a public way. And I'm so proud to do so. I'm so proud to be able to help others and just share my truth, my story. And I'm not ashamed of it. I just want to shine a light on how good your life can get when you can be free of addiction."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Brandy Ledford told Fox News Digital she continues to lean on her personal relationship with God. (Matt Kallish)
Ledford said sobriety didn't just transform her life. It also strengthened her relationship with God.

"My relationship with God has helped shape this new chapter in my life by listening to His will, by turning my will and my life over to God," she said. "Any time I have a decision to make, I lean on my faith to help me find the answers. I pause instead of making rash decisions, and ... I have even more trust that the answers will come.
Brandy Ledford attends the 30th anniversary of "Baywatch" at the Viceroy Hotel in Santa Monica, Calif., Sept. 24, 2019. (Presley Ann/Getty Images)

"There's an expression: 'Trust God, clean house,'" she beamed. "I didn't know that before I got sober, but I always talked about how much faith I had. Faith and trust are so different, and it's such a layered concept."
Brandy Ledford attends the premiere of ABC News Studios docuseries "After Baywatch: Moment in the Sun" at The Bungalow on Aug. 26, 2024, in Santa Monica, Calif. (Variety via Getty Images)
Ledford said she has developed a deeper understanding of her relationship with God by learning to trust Him while remaining true to herself.
The desire to connect with others has also shaped Ledford’s latest venture. As a creator on Passes, she said the platform allows her to build meaningful relationships with fans on her own terms.
Brandy Ledford splits her time between Los Angeles, Vancouver and Kauai. (Amanda Edwards/Getty Images)
The site lets celebrities, athletes and digital creators share content and interact directly with subscribers.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Today, Brandy Ledford is also a wellness advocate. (Courtesy of Brandy Ledford)

"I don't answer my DMs on Instagram, TikTok or Twitter (now X) only because I get a lot of them," she said. "It's not personal. But in this way, I feel like I get to have a relationship with fans, and they get to know the real me.

"I get to really connect on a one-on-one level, but I also get to be my full self and benefit from it, benefit from being who I want to be without somebody dictating how they think it should be. And it's fun. It's a really fun way to share my life with others and connect.
Brandy Ledford stays in shape as a yoga teacher. (Presley Ann/Getty Images for Baby2Baby)

"My whole idea of connection is the opposite of addiction," she said. "And to be able to connect with people in a one-on-one way and to really be free to do so, it's kind of brilliant. I love this new world, with us getting to be in control, getting to be in charge and still being super creative."

These days, Ledford is embracing a new chapter. In addition to doing voiceover work for "King of the Hill," she serves on the board of the Red Songbird Foundation, a nonprofit founded in 2009 by singer Hilary Roberts, who has been sober from drugs and alcohol since 1997. The organization provides support for people struggling with trauma, mental health challenges, substance abuse disorder and PTSD.
Brandy Ledford hopes her story will inspire others struggling to turn their lives around. (Matt Kallish)
"I'm really proud to be in a position where I can do things that help others," Ledford said. "I just want to continue."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Meghan Markle's 'MasterChef Australia' controversy may be exactly the point: experts
summary: Meghan Markle's "MasterChef Australia" guest judge role sparks boycott calls and praise as royal experts debate whether the appearance can reset her brand.
story: Royal broadcaster Neil Sean discusses an interview given by Angela Kelly, Queen Elizabeths long-time dresser and best friend regarding conflicts within the palace including tension surrounding Meghan Markle and Prince Harrys wedding.
Meghan Markle's upcoming appearance on "MasterChef Australia" has already sparked debate, with royal experts telling Fox News Digital the backlash may be just as important as the episode itself.

The hit reality cooking series announced in an Instagram post that the 44-year-old Duchess of Sussex would be joining the show as a guest judge for Sunday's episode, writing that Markle will be "bringing her love of food, entertaining and seasonal produce to one of the competition's most memorable challenges."
In a press release, Markle, who filmed the episode during her visit to Australia with her husband Prince Harry in April, explained why she wanted to take part in the episode.
'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS
"What attracted me to the MasterChef Australia kitchen? Two things: my love of food and my love of Australia. It was an easy yes," Markle said.
Meghan Markle's upcoming role as a guest judge on "MasterChef Australia" sparked praise and backlash.  (Getty Images)
"It’s such a great show," she continued. "I’m just really honored that I was asked to be able to be here with you and to be able to judge some of these meals."
The press release noted that the cooks will take on the challenge of creating "a dish fit for a Duchess" using some of Markle's "favorite seasonal ingredients."
MEGHAN MARKLE'S SHOW EMMY NOMINATION 'SOMEWHAT BAFFLING' DUE TO LACKLUSTER RATINGS: EXPERT
In a preview of the episode that appeared on Sydney's 10 News, Markle appeared alongside season 18 "MasterChef Australia" judges Poh Ling Yeow, Sofia Levin and Jean-Christophe Novelli.
Markle introduced her chosen ingredients, noting that the chefs had "quite the bounty her" and proudly sharing that her children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, "eat Brussels sprouts."
"That’s impressive," Levin said.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S HOLLYWOOD DREAMS HIT WALL AS EXPERT WARNS OF ‘TOXIC BRAND’ STIGMA

"Food and cooking to me is really a love language," Markle explained later in the preview. "I think it’s such a great way to connect. It’s something that can feel sentimental and meaningful and It’s how I, it’s how I show my nurturing and love for my friends, family, and my kids."
The duchess will appear in Sunday's episode of the cooking competition show.  (Netflix)

Following the announcement, Markle's participation in "MasterChef Australia" was quickly met with a divided reaction on social media, earning both praise from supporters and calls for a boycott from critics.
"Why? She’s not a chef??? Not interested!" one Instagram user wrote.
"Can't stand her. She's not a chef," another agreed, adding, "Why is she even on this show."
"Thanks for the heads-up and making it easier to avoid," one critic commented as another chimed in, "Definitely won't watch it!"
"First time since the beginning of this show, that I WON’T be watching, first time!!" another detractor wrote.
Markle recently earned her first Daytime Emmy Award nomination for "With Love, Meghan." (Jake Rosenberg/Netflix © 2025)
However, others expressed their excitement over seeing Markle's appearance.
"Can’t wait to watch it!!!" one social media user commented.
"I'll be WATCHING!!" another added.
"I know she will do a great job," a fan enthused.
"I CAN'T WAIT!! WE LOVE YOU PRINCESS MEGHAN," another supporter wrote.
"I love this for her… she is working and finding opportunities for herself," one fan added.
"All the people saying they won’t watch are the first ones who will be watching and later criticizing," another commenter wrote. "I can’t wait to watch! Love Meghan!"
Markle's appearance also made headlines and fueled debate online after a report claimed her team requested that she not be referred to as "royalty" during filming.
Royal expert Richard Fitzwilliam said the controversy around her appearance could be exactly the point.  (Netflix)
The polarized reaction to Markle's latest gig underscores a familiar pattern for the Duchess of Sussex, whose post-royal ventures have often generated as much controversy as publicity.

Royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital the attention surrounding Markle's appearance, whether positive or negative, could ultimately benefit both the duchess and the cooking competition.
"Every time Meghan’s name gets in the papers, even if it is negative, it builds up the power of her brand," he said. "It also helps to hype the show before it starts."
"She was chosen as a guest judge to boost the ratings of the show," Fitzwilliams added.

While Markle's role has prompted questions about her qualifications, British broadcaster Helena Chard argued that professional cooking experience isn't necessarily a requirement for a celebrity guest judge.
"I don’t believe she’s a qualified chef. But then, they’ve had Steve Irwin as a guest judge before and he wasn’t a chef either," she pointed out. "So it’s not really about culinary credentials."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

The "Suits" alum's guest judging stint marks her latest foray into the food and lifestyle world. In March 2025, Markle's "With Love, Meghan" lifestyle and reality show premiered on Netflix. In the show, Meghan shared cooking, gardening and entertaining tips alongside celebrity guests. "With Love, Meghan" also served as a launchpad for her As Ever lifestyle brand.

In January 2026, Netflix reportedly canceled the show after two seasons and later announced that it was ending its partnership with the As Ever brand though Markle and Prince Harry retained a first-look production deal with the streamer. However, "With Love, Meghan" recently received a surprise Daytime Emmy Award nomination for outstanding lifestyle series. "Meghan does have an interest in food and entertaining," Chard noted. "So from a PR perspective, appearing on ‘MasterChef Australia’ alongside well-known hosts, strengthens her brand."
Fitzwilliams argued that Markle's involvement could boost ratings.  (Netflix)

While Chard saw the guest judging role as a natural fit, other royal experts told Fox News Digital that the response illustrates the challenges Markle continues to face with public perception after stepping away from royal life.

"People are talking more about why she's judging than what she's judging," royal reporter Kinsey Schofield said. "An image reset only works if the audience buys into the new image, and right now many viewers still see a disconnect between Meghan's branding and her actual experience or authority in this space."

"Social media always amplifies the loudest voices," the "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" host continued. "That said, there does seem to be a broader sense of Meghan fatigue. Every project arrives carrying years of baggage, and that's a challenge most celebrities simply don't have. She isn't launching from a blank slate. She's launching from a very divided public reputation."
Fitzwilliams agreed, saying there have been "sufferers from Meghan fatigue for some time" and that "a great many viewers feel this way."

"Lifestyle is aspirational, it's lucrative, and it gives celebrities tremendous control over their image," Schofield said. "The problem is that audiences don't just buy recipes or table settings anymore. They're buying authenticity."
Other experts warned that the appearance could "backfire." (Netflix)
Fitzwilliams shared his view that Markle's cameo is also tied to her broader business ambitions. "She is returning to food in the hope this boosts sales of the As Ever products," he said.
Schofield said that the guest judge appearance may not deliver the hoped-for results, arguing that every project that Markle takes on is now judged through the lens of the duchess herself.

"Meghan has had several opportunities to reinvent herself since leaving royal life, and the pattern has remained the same… enormous publicity followed by polarized reactions," she told Fox News Digital. "One television appearance probably won't rewrite that narrative overnight."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"People often react to the brand before they react to the product," she added. "That's the downside of building such a personality-driven business model. Every project becomes less about the content itself and more about whether people have bought into Meghan as the person selling it."
Experts questioned whether audiences would see Markle as a credible judge of the contestants' dishes.  (Getty Images)
Beyond the public reaction, some royal experts questioned whether audiences would view her as a credible choice to critique contestants on "MasterChef Australia."

"Celebrity guest judges aren't expected to have Michelin stars, but they do need to bring something credible to the table," Schofield said. "Meghan's challenge is that she's still trying to establish herself as an authority in this space while much of the audience sees her as someone playing a part."
Royal expert Hilary Fordwich shared her opinion that Markle's divisive public image makes her guest appearance different from most casting decisions.

"Meghan is so polarizing that while such an appearance would be low-risk for any regular celebrity, it is likely to backfire," she said, adding that the duchess "has no credentials" and "doesn't come across as authentic."
"Given the failure of her previous cooking attempts, with lackluster ratings, this is all she can do now which is to be involved in a show which is already a success," Fordwich said.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex is pictured at the Hubb Community Kitchen in London on Nov. 21, 2018 to celebrate the success of their cookbook. The kitchen was set up by women affected by the Grenfell tower fire, and the duchess wrote a foreword to the cookbook to help raise funds for the victims. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
However, royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner shared a more optimistic outlook on Markle's latest endeavor.

"Meghan is a master at reinventions, keeping herself in the public eye, and ‘MasterChef Australia’ is the latest platform to succumb to the real values of the lady and obviously cooking is one of many talents," he said.

Turner pointed to Markle's previous charitable work with the Hubb Community Kitchen, which was established in the wake of London's devastating Grenfell Tower fire. In June 2017, a fire ignited in the 24-story Grenfell Tower apartment block which killed 72 people and displaced hundreds of residents. After becoming involved with the community kitchen in 2018, Markle cooked alongside local women and helped publish a charity cookbook that raised money to support the initiative.
The royal expert told Fox News Digital that he also believed Markle would resonate with Australian audiences.
"Australia is a country which values people who have initiative and drive, and Meghan has that people's touch to support and offer cookery as one of her skill bases," he said.
Royal expert Ian Pelham Turner said Markle is a "master at reinventions." (Netflix)
For all the debate surrounding Markle's guest judging role, experts said the real question is whether the attention translates into viewers.
Schofield believes Markle's appearance could prove beneficial for "MasterChef Australia" if the buzz prompts audiences to tune in.

"Meghan guarantees headlines, and headlines translate into curiosity," she said. "Whether that curiosity becomes ratings or resentment is the million-dollar question. Producers know controversy can be good for television, but only if viewers stay for the episode instead of switching it off."

title: Ben Affleck and Casey Affleck's mom, Chris Anne Affleck, dead at 83 after pancreatic cancer battle
summary: Chris Anne Affleck was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in December 2025 and given six months to live. Her obituary reveals a touching final wish.
story: Ben Affleck, who stars in and directs "AIR," explained at a press conference that he met with the NBA legend before getting started on the film.
Ben Affleck and Casey Affleck's mom has died following a battle with cancer.
According to an obituary published in The Boston Globe on Friday, Christopher Anne Affleck, died peacefully in her sleep on June 2 at the age of 83.
The Hollywood Reporter reported she was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in December 2025, and was given six months to live.

"Her greatest wish after her diagnosis, however, was to live to see her grandson graduate high school," the obituary reads. "She did so, attending with her family on May 31, 2026. She died peacefully, in her sleep, two days later."
Ben Affleck and Casey Affleck's mother, Chris, died at the age of 83 in June. (Bill Brett/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
HOLLYWOOD STARS WHO DIED IN 2026

Born in 1942 in New York City, Chris proved to be a great activist, teaching "literacy classes in Mississippi during Freedom Summer, marched against the Vietnam War, and reveled in 1960s counterculture."
She went on to become "one of the first Radcliffe women" to graduate from Harvard, and spent 35 years as a public school teacher.
"Every student, whether just arrived from Haiti or Cambridge upper crust, was a cherished citizen of her classroom republic, equal to each other and to herself," the obituary states.

After working as a teacher for over three decades, Chris retired in 2008, spending time volunteering for President Barack Obama during his campaign, traveling to Israel/Palestine and becoming an organizer for the Alliance for Water Justice in Palestine.
Chris welcomed Ben in 1972 and Casey in 1975 with her ex-husband, Timothy Affleck. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)
Chris welcomed Ben in 1972 and Casey in 1975, with her ex-husband, Timothy Affleck, before they divorced in 1984.

Both Ben and Casey credit their parents with instilling in them a love for the arts at a young age, with Casey telling Collider in 2013 that they "started out as children doing this" in part because their "father was in the theater and our mother took us to the theater all the time."

"I got into acting as a young child on account of a sort of arbitrary thing. A friend of my mom’s was a casting director so, really as kind of a lark," Ben told Parade in October 2007. "I had a couple of acting jobs that had just enough exposure to give me the option to continue if I wanted to. I followed through with it."
Ben later had his big break when he won the Academy Award for best original screenplay in 1998, alongside Matt Damon, for their work writing "Good Will Hunting."
Ben and Casey credit their parents for instilling a love of art in them from a young age. (BG004/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Both Ben and Damon brought their mothers with them as their plus-ones for the big ceremony.

"We were sitting next to our moms, and we won, and we kind of hugged our moms. I remember how everyone had made such a big thing out of it as if this was such a novelty," Ben told Vanity Fair in April 2023. "I remember thinking, being insecure, like, ‘Why? Why is it weird that we’re bringing our moms?’ Who else do you think we would bring?"
He continued, "There was nobody else that was going to go. That was it. Of course, our moms were gonna go. That was really innocent and not faked."

Ben Affleck couldn't understand why others were confused about why he brought his mom as his plus one to the Oscars. (Ke.Mazur/WireImage)

title: Paul Anka slams modern singers, says Frank Sinatra would have 'thrown a chair'
summary: Paul Anka says Frank Sinatra would have thrown a chair if asked to use autotune, praising an era when singers had to perform live until perfect.
story: The legendary singer-songwriter discusses his HBO film "Paul Anka: His Way," his song-writing legacy including writing "My Way" for Frank Sinatra, and his upcoming album.
Paul Anka slammed modern singers and the technology that helps them sound better, saying Franka Sinatra would have thrown a chair at someone if they asked him to use autotune.
Anka called Sinatra and Elvis Presley his two "towers" of music while speaking to Billy Corgan of the Smashing Pumpkins on his "The Magnificent Others" podcast this week.
"When Elvis was around, he just – they both owned a room, and they were both given that it factor," he explained.
FRANK SINATRA'S DESERT HIDEAWAY WAS 'ALL SEX, ALL THE TIME,' FORMER VALET CLAIMS
Paul Anka is seen performing in New York City in 2008. (WireImage)

He added, "And Elvis worked his a-- off. This was a shy guy. I would sit with him like this: ‘Hey, Paulie,’" he said in a reserved imitation of Presley. "‘How you doing, man? Yeah, Paul. You know, one day I'm going to do that "My Way." I love that "My Way."’"
He said he told Presley that he wouldn’t want to cover the song made famous by Sinatra because it wasn’t exactly his style of music.
"But what an amazing force to watch and be around it," he continued.
The "Put Your Head on My Shoulder" singer said he and Presley learned that it "wasn't about just getting up there and singing. You had to entertain people."
Frank Sinatra is seen performing at the United Cerebral Palsy telethon at the studios of KECA-TV in Los Angeles in 1952. (Getty Images)

The 84-year-old gave the example of the notoriously unpredictable Bob Dylan, whom he admits he loves, but said would sometimes go on stage and "couldn’t give a s--- and people walk out, ‘What the f---?’ If you don't entertain people, you're dead."
Regarding Sinatra, he vowed the "Fly Me to the Moon" crooner "will get bigger, young people will learn exactly what true quality is, you know, at a time when there was no autotune."

"Think about the difference. I don't know who the f--- is doing the singing today. Do you?" he admitted. "Can you imagine back then if you said to Sinatra, ‘We're going to give you an autotune’? He would have thrown a chair at you."
Singers in Sinatra’s time, he said, "walked in a studio after rehearsing, as I stated earlier, and you kept singing, and that band kept playing till you got perfect."

Elvis Presley is seen singing in front of a mob of fans in 1957. (Getty Images)
"That was it," he continued. "And he was the guy."
Anka said Sinatra set the standard and "made it tough for anybody to ever stand in front of a band again. We all came second, but he was the guy we emulated."
He also said that Sammy Davis, Jr. was the most "short-changed" on being recognized.
"To Frank and Dean [Martin] and to all of us, he was the most talented," Anka said.

"That was the most talented guy," he professed. "He was a musician. He played drums. He played this, he did that. He sang great. He was the guy that I hope today somehow they put him back in the forefront. And Dean was an underrated singer."
Anka said he was impressed with Michael Jackson's talent when he worked with him. (Getty Images)
Anka said a specific song that he wrote for Davis but didn't name was "as important to me as ‘My Way’ with Sinatra."

Anka wrote "My Way" for Sinatra in 1968.

title: Jon Bon Jovi abruptly ends Madison Square Garden show after health setback
summary: Jon Bon Jovi stopped his Madison Square Garden residency show after just 90 minutes due to a health issue, with Train frontman Pat Monahan stepping in to help.
story: Jon Bon Jovi was singing "Living on a Prayer" at his Madison Square Garden concert when he had Pat Monahan take over the vocals before ending the concert early.

Jon Bon Jovi unexpectedly cut his Madison Square Garden concert short Thursday night after appearing to have difficulty getting through the performance – forcing Train frontman Pat Monahan to step in and help carry the show across the finish line.
A representative for Bon Jovi confirmed to Fox News Digital that the concert ended early, saying the singer told fans from the stage he had been battling a health setback.
"Jon Bon Jovi spoke from stage and told fans he has been battling a sinus infection which led to the show's early ending," the representative said in a statement.
ROD STEWART CANCELS LAS VEGAS CONCERT HOURS BEFORE SHOWTIME ON DOCTOR'S ORDERS
The shortened show marks a setback in Jon Bon Jovi's comeback following 2022 vocal cord surgery that nearly ended his performing career permanently. (John Nacion/Getty Images)
"As part of the Bon Jovi residency at Madison Square Garden, Jon has said numerous times that it has been a joy to return to live shows for the band. Updated information will be available shortly."
An insider who attended the concert told Fox News Digital Bon Jovi performed for roughly 90 minutes.

Bon Jovi's previous Madison Square Garden residency shows have lasted over two hours, the insider noted. Thursday's performance wrapped after approximately 15 songs, ending far earlier than fans had come to expect.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Jon Bon Jovi performs onstage during Bon Jovi's Forever Tour at Madison Square Garden on July 21, 2026, in New York City. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Bon Jovi)
Monahan was in the arena as a fan Thursday night and was not part of the scheduled show, according to the insider.
WATCH: JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY CUTS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN CONCERT SHORT

The 64-year-old rocker was performing on night eight of his nine-show residency when he stopped the show early. Monahan joined him for "Livin' on a Prayer," taking over the vocals midway through the song.
The shortened performance comes as Bon Jovi continues his comeback following vocal cord surgery in 2022. This is his first major tour since undergoing the career-saving procedure.

Just months before launching the "Forever Tour," Bon Jovi admitted he had been prepared to walk away from music after a vocal cord injury left him fearing he could never perform at the level fans expected.
Jon Bon Jovi cut his performance short after battling a sinus infection. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Bon Jovi)
In October 2025, Bon Jovi recalled realizing something was wrong after a 15-show run.
At the end of the final show, he told his wife he thought it was "pretty good," but his wife disagreed, Bon Jovi recalled on the "How to Fail" podcast.
"I don't think I could do this anymore. I don't know why, but I'm OK with walking away from this because there's no way I'm dragging down the legacy," Bon Jovi said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Doctors later discovered the source of the problem.
"I sought out a surgeon who explained to me that one of my vocal cords had literally atrophied," Bon Jovi said. "It was dying."
He underwent surgery and received an implant designed to help his vocal cords close properly.
Jon Bon Jovi abruptly ended his Madison Square Garden residency. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)
"If I worked hard, he promised me nothing other than I would be better than I was that night in Nashville," Bon Jovi explained.
Still, the road to recovery wasn't easy.

"Had I known that it was going to be a three-and-a-half-year recovery, I very well might have said thank you, good night," he said. "But the process and the progress was steady enough that I didn't lose faith."
By the time he announced the "Forever Tour," Bon Jovi said he felt "close enough to fully recovered" to return to the stage.
"I'm not doing this for the applause. I'm not doing it for the money. I'm not doing it the fame," he said. "I've had enough of all of it.

"But I would like to feel that joy and the resonance, even if it were only one last time. I don't think this is anywhere near a farewell tour or anything like that. But if it were, you could trust that these few shows that I've announced are gonna be joy-filled."
The "Forever Tour" began July 7 with a nine-show residency at Madison Square Garden and is scheduled to wrap Sept. 9 at London's Wembley Stadium.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Playboy's celebrity-driven relaunch faces credibility test in OnlyFans era, expert says
summary: Karol G and Cara Delevingne front Playboy's celebrity-driven relaunch as new editor Philip Picardi pivots to prestige storytelling.
story: "Baywatch" actress Donna D'Errico posed for the cover of Playboy in 1995 and thought it would be "kind of cool" to get to do it again.
Playboy is back on the rack, now with a focus on "prestige" and storytelling alongside the nude images synonymous with the magazine.

More than 70 years after Hugh Hefner founded the men's magazine brand, newly-appointed editor-in-chief Philip Picardi and David Miller, Playboy’s president of media and brand, were tasked with reviving the publication for an ever-changing audience.

A celebrity-focused relaunch to promote the iconic Playboy Playmates and Bunnies began in April with Colombian pop star Karol G on the cover. The sold-out print run lead efforts for a larger print run of its latest issue featuring supermodel Cara Delevingne in only a latex corset.
HOLLY MADISON SAYS PLAYBOY MANSION FELT LIKE A 'SAFE HARBOR' AFTER SHE ENCOUNTERED HOLLYWOOD'S DARK SIDE
Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that it's essential for Playboy to evolve if they want to survive a reinvention.

Hugh Hefner branded the Playboy Bunny, a formally-trained cocktail waitress in a specific uniform at the members-only event at the Playboy Club in 1960. (Photo by Ted West/Central Press/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

"It's not about erasing who you were — it's about carrying the core of what made you iconic into a context that makes sense today," Uthe said. "Playboy knows what it is. The question is whether it can translate that into something the market is ready to receive."
CARA DELEVINGNE ISSUES STARK WARNING AFTER TERRIFYING DRUG ADDICTION

Picardi recently told the Press Gazette that focusing on what "initially drove its prestige and its buzz and its interest and its loyalty, which was of course its storytelling" was paramount for Playboy's revival.
"Playboy knows what it is. The question is whether it can translate that into something the market is ready to receive."

"There’s always been a difference between Playboy and porn, especially the kinds of porn that are really prevalent today and that people have access to just by having a Twitter account or a Reddit account," Picardi told the outlet. "And so I actually found the challenge of bringing back an artfulness and a thoughtfulness to nudity to be super exciting as a creative."

In addition to featuring Playmates of the month, photoshoots are featured online and across social media platforms. Picardi also admitted that cover stars are "fully involved" in the creative process, including approval over photographers and stylists.
'BAYWATCH' STAR DONNA D'ERRICO SAYS PLAYBOY REJECTED HER 30 YEARS AFTER PROVOCATIVE COVER
"I stop short of calling what we do at Playboy feminist, because I think that’s a loaded term, and I’m sure many people would disagree with that qualification," Picardi said.
'BAYWATCH' STAR CARMEN ELECTRA SHARES WHAT MEN MUST AVOID WHEN PURSUING MIDDLE-AGED WOMEN

"But what I will say is what our approach with nudity has always been: that it is up to a woman how much she has to show on set … when we make sure that the permission lies with the woman herself, we’re always surprised that she feels very liberated to make the calls and do what she wants to do, which is often showing more than we expected or thought of."
Playboy was once one of the most influential print publications. (Getty Images)
Uthe agreed that power dynamics were still very much in play, albeit with unbalanced scales.

"The cultural headwinds are real — but they're not as uniformly strong as people assume," Uthe said. "Yes, #MeToo shifted the conversation around how women are viewed. But look at OnlyFans: over 300 million registered users, creators earning billions annually.
"The appetite for adult content and sexual expression didn't disappear — it just moved, and in many cases toward platforms where women hold the power."
PLAYMATE OF THE YEAR FOR PLAYBOY MAGAZINE COMEBACK SAYS ONLYFANS IS NO COMPETITION

She added, "That's actually Playboy's opening if they're smart enough to take it. The challenge isn't the market. The challenge is credibility. Can Playboy convince a generation that grew up with creator-controlled content that a legacy brand can authentically stand for the same thing?"
Celebrity partnerships may be "critical" at this stage in the game, but Uthe warned it only works if "the alignment is real."

"The challenge isn't the market. The challenge is credibility. Can Playboy convince a generation that grew up with creator-controlled content that a legacy brand can authentically stand for the same thing?"
Hugh Hefner launched Playboy in the 1950s. (HECTOR MATA/AFP via Getty Images)
"Karol G and Cara Delevingne aren't random choices, and that's the point," she said. "Every partnership is a positioning signal right now. The danger is chasing names instead of synonymy.
"The partners need to embody what Playboy is becoming, not just lend their audience to it. Done right, this accelerates everything. Done wrong, it reads as desperate."
FORMER PLAYBOY MODEL HOLLY MADISON ADMITS BEDROOM ACTIVITIES SHE DIDN'T LIKE TO DO WITH HUGH HEFNER
Despite heightened interest in publishing a new version of past pleasures, the brand still has an uphill battle.

"Playboy should show, not tell," Uthe said. "There's something worth saving — the cultural footprint, the iconography, the permission to talk about sexuality openly and unapologetically. But hope isn't a strategy."
The Playboy Club launched in Chicago in 1960 and expanded with a total of 33 locations. (Photo by Keystone Features/Getty Images)
"The brands that make it back are the ones that stop defending their legacy and start building the next chapter. Playboy has the name. The question is whether they have the discipline to survive."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
The once-monthly print magazine went quarterly in 2019 and then shuttered in March 2020 during the pandemic. Special print issues were released before CEO Ben Kohn brought in a new team.
In 2025, the company made $120.9 million, with a net loss of $12.7 million, compared to $79.4 million in 2024, according to an earnings release.
Dolly Parton famously posed for a portrait session dressed as a playboy bunny in 1978. (Harry Langdon/Getty Images)
Pamela Anderson holds the Playboy cover record with 14 appearances. (Getty Images)

Miller said there's interest in reviving Playboy-style parties, sporting events and research, but that they still want to make the brand "respectful, and we want to make it modern, and feel like it’s inviting and inclusive for all individuals."
Media executive Derek Reisfield, who previously served as CBS's vice president of business development, noted that Hefner was "very creative" about his brand growth and distribution.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"He had the Playboy clubs ... It was a lifestyle thing," Reisfeld told Fox News Digital. "They had licensing, which is almost pure profit. The magazine was this great engine that then also enabled them to get into filmed entertainment with the Playboy Channel."
Anna Nicole Smith was Playmate of the Year for Playboy. (Getty Images)

He added, "But the Internet came along and basically blew all these guys out of the water because there was a proliferation of pornography and semi-pornography, and it was all accessible. It was pretty cheap and and so that sort of killed it.
"They're trying to figure out how do I thread the needle in this new world where all this stuff is available to people and a lot of it's not really differentiated."
Celebrities and earned media appear to be the driving force for the business, which Reisfield admitted was "difficult positioning" for the publication.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"You have to get it just right, and I don't know if they have," he said. "I would want to do very extensive research about who the customer is, what trade-offs they're making, what their current media habits are, where there's an opening and where the heritage of Playboy can be deployed.
He added, "It's got to be true to the brand or what people believe the brand is."
Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

title: 'Ransom Canyon' star Josh Duhamel says he'd rather put money into North Dakota after selling Los Angeles home
summary: Josh Duhamel splits time between Fargo and Los Angeles while raising his family off the grid, revealing how ranch life informs his Netflix role.
story: The "Ransom Canyon" star recently sold one of his Los Angeles homes, choosing instead to invest his money in his new homebase, Fargo, North Dakota.
Josh Duhamel is ready to set down roots somewhere other than Los Angeles.
In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 53-year-old actor discussed season two of "Ransom Canyon," as well as his decision to sell his LA home following his move to North Dakota.

"Well, we still have a house in Los Angeles that we have because I have a 12-year-old son who goes to school there and will be there until he's done with school," he said. "So we go back and forth between Fargo, North Dakota and Los Angeles. The house that I just sold was the house that was sort of my transition space between when I got divorced and when I started a new family."
He explained that after "renting it for the last couple of years," he decided to sell it, adding, he realized he would "rather put that money in North Dakota."

‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’

In addition to allowing his family to "get back to the basics," and his children to grow up exploring nature rather than being on their iPads all day, Duhamel says living an off-the-grid lifestyle in their Minnesota getaway has helped him prepare for his role in "Ransom Canyon."

title: Oprah Winfrey sparks fresh backlash after she revisits Prince Harry and Meghan Markle bombshell interview
summary: Oprah Winfrey explains her unscripted "silent or silenced" question to Meghan Markle as critics accuse her of rewriting history years later.
story: Hugo Vickers, author of "Queen Elizabeth II: A Personal History," details how the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's exit and Oprah interview added strain during the late monarch's final years.
Oprah Winfrey is facing a new wave of backlash over an old royal bombshell.
After revisiting her 2021 interview with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, Winfrey's explanation of her "silent or silenced" question has sparked renewed debate online.

The media mogul's reflection on one of the most talked-about moments from the explosive sit-down has reignited debate over the interview that shook the monarchy, divided viewers and put Harry and Meghan's claims about royal life under a global microscope.
MEGHAN MARKLE, PRINCE HARRY'S INTERVIEW WITH OPRAH WINFREY: 6 BIGGEST BOMBSHELLS
Oprah Winfrey interviewed Prince Harry and Meghan Markle for a special in 2021 where they revealed their struggles with royal life. (Harpo Productions/Joe Pugliese via Getty Images)

During a recent Vanity Fair interview, Winfrey looked back on the viral exchange with Meghan, explaining why she challenged the Duchess of Sussex after she said she had been "silent" during her time as a working royal.

"I wanted to be clear because was she silenced? Were people telling her not to talk?... I said it for clarification because I didn't want later to hear, 'Well, no, it wasn't that. It really was that I was silenced. They wouldn't let me talk.' So it was all for clarification."
Meghan told Winfrey at the time, "I've always valued independence" and "I've always been outspoken, especially about women's rights."
"I mean, that's the sad irony of the last four years is I've advocated for so long for women to use their voice. And then, I was silent."
Winfrey responded with the question that instantly went viral.
"Were you silent or were you silenced?"
"The latter," Meghan replied.
Winfrey also revealed that Harry and Meghan did not know what questions she planned to ask before the interview.
"They didn't know obviously anything that I was going to ask them, but I had said to them ahead of time, 'I'm going to try to cover everything.'"
"This interview took three and a half hours... I was just trying to carefully go through everything that had come up in the past."
Oprah Winfrey sparks royal backlash after revisiting her viral 'silenced' question to Meghan Markle. (Chris Jackson - Pool/Getty Images)

The 2021 CBS special became one of the biggest celebrity interviews of the decade after Harry and Meghan opened up about their decision to step away from royal duties, allegations of a lack of support from the royal family, Meghan's mental health struggles, and claims about conversations surrounding their son Archie's royal status and security.
The couple's comments sparked worldwide debate, including Meghan's claim that there were "concerns and conversations" about "how dark his skin might be when he's born."
Harry also described feeling trapped within the royal institution.
"I need to do this for my family. This is not a surprise to anybody," he said.
QUEEN ELIZABETH CALLS FOR UNITY AHEAD OF MEGHAN MARKLE, PRINCE HARRY INTERVIEW IN COMMONWEALTH DAY SPEECH
"It's really sad that it's got to this point, but I've got to do something for my own mental health, for my wife's, and for Archie's as well, because I could see where this was headed."
Winfrey's latest comments quickly triggered a wave of reactions online.
"Oprah backpedaling?" one X user wrote.

Another critic commented, "Oh, Oprah… You failed to challenge obvious inconsistencies… and handed Harry and Meghan a worldwide stage to tell 'their story' without proper scrutiny or questioning. Now you want 'clarification?' That ship sailed! Spare me…"
Oprah Winfrey reignites backlash over the bombshell Prince Harry royal interview. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

But supporters pushed back against the criticism.
"In that royal climate she was silenced she didn't have a voice. The royals can't express their own opinions, everyone knows that," one Instagram user wrote.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle sit with their son Archie during their 2019 tour in Cape Town, South Africa.  (Samir Hussein)

title: Michael J. Fox says going public with Parkinson's was 'hell' on wife Tracy Pollan
summary: Michael J. Fox reveals the toll going public with his Parkinson's diagnosis has taken on wife Tracy Pollan and why he refused to hide his condition from the world.
story: Deborah W. Brooks told Fox News Digital the foundation has ‘committed over $3 billion dollars worth of research worldwide.’
Michael J. Fox is opening up about how going public with his battle with Parkinson's has affected not only him, but his loved ones.

As part of the third annual Social Impact Summit, hosted by The Hollywood Reporter and Social Impact Fund, the 65-year-old actor went into detail about why he chose to go public with his Parkinson's diagnosis and the toll that decision had and continues to have on his family, particularly his wife, Tracy Pollan.

"It was hell on Tracy. It was really hard on her — and it still is, because it’s always changing," he told The Hollywood Reporter. "But I said to her, ‘I have to go all the way here. No half measures.’
VINCE GILL GAVE AMY GRANT A REALITY CHECK DURING RECOVERY FROM BRAIN INJURY

"I started to understand what it was like for these people who didn’t have the options or the choices I had, didn’t have the connections and the reason to be optimistic ... I needed to normalize it and just be that all the time. I said, ‘I have to not hide this. F--- vanity.’"

The actor was first diagnosed with the degenerative disease in 1991 at the age of 29, keeping his diagnosis a secret for seven years, before going public in 1998 during the third season of his hit show, "Spin City."
Fox said his decision to go public with his Parkinson's diagnosis was "hell" for his wife. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images for The Michael J. Fox Foundation)

After one more season on the show, Fox chose to retire from acting to devote his time to advocacy and raising money for Parkinson's disease. It was then that he founded The Michael J. Fox Foundation in 2000, which is dedicated to finding a cure.

Since its inception, the foundation has generated more than $3 billion for research, which has left Fox and Deborah W. Brooks, co-Founder and CEO of the foundation, optimistic about where the research is headed.
WATCH: Co-founder of The Michael J. Fox Foundation is proud of what they have achieved

"Well, it's been the best state for Parkinson's research ever," Brooks said. "And, in large part, so much of that progress has taken place in the course of our organization's existence. Not that we're responsible for everything, but we've scaled so significantly and have been able to activate scientists globally. And that is showing in the results and the pace of progress across our field.

"We have now committed over $3 billion worth of research worldwide, and, so, we're working with scientists everywhere, and we work with academics, biotechs and pharma. Our goal is to take aha moments and get them to the drugstore shelf.

"And, so, it's been that momentum and particularly a recent breakthrough in how we can detect Parkinson's even before symptoms are the kind of things that tell us. We are onto it, and we are not giving up."
Brooks credits Fox for his courage to live his life with Parkinson's in front of the world. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
Brooks credits Fox for his "courage and willingness to live his Parkinson's experience in front of the world," calling it "empowering for patients who face similar experiences in reducing stigma."

She also recalled her first board meeting at the foundation, noting it was clear Fox was not one to "just to put his name on something and hope for the best," and that his goal has always been "to do everything it took and get this done and close our doors."
WATCH: Deborah W. Brooks commends Michael J. Fox for his 'courage' to live openly with Parkinson's

"His purity of motive has been core to helping us think what we're going to prioritize. It shapes our values in terms of speed. Something like trying to cure diseases, that's not a time-neutral agenda item for people who have degenerative and progressive disease. And, so, I think, you know, this notion that someone puts their voice out or lends their name, it's always been deeper than that for him.

"And I see that a lot more in philanthropy in general today, but it has been a game changer. For raising awareness, of course, but it's also been a game changer to put those values to work in our mission to cure Parkinson's disease."
Brooks has seen firsthand how Fox's decision to go public with his diagnosis has helped others, saying she gets emotional thinking about his interactions with other patients.
"It is so powerful, an experience to be seen and felt when you share the experience of Parkinson's disease," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Fox initially retired from acting in 1998 but has since returned and is now nominated for an Emmy. (Savion Washington/FilmMagic)

While the "Back to the Future" star initially retired from acting in 1998, he returned in his first major on-screen role in 2004 for a guest appearance in "Scrubs," later starring in "The Good Wife," "Boston Legal" and "Curb Your Enthusiasm."

"It’s really prolonged my life and made my life interesting in a way that I didn’t think it would be to this point," Fox told The Hollywood Reporter. "I’m not retired from acting, but if I didn’t act again, it would be for a very good reason. I let Parkinson’s make decisions for me."
WATCH: Deborah W. Brooks gets choked up when thinking of Michael J. Fox interacting with patients
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Most recently, Fox received an Emmy nomination for his guest role on the hit Apple TV+ show, "Shrinking," in which he played a man dealing with Parkinson's who meets Harrison Ford's character, who has also been diagnosed with the disease, in a doctor's office.

"He was happy that I was sharing my experience with him as a character and helping him do what he needed to do," Fox explained. "He was so loving. I didn’t know what to expect with Harrison because he’s famously a stoic, curmudgeonly guy, and he’s really a sweetheart. He was so affectionate to me and so welcoming to me."
Fox guest starred on "Shrinking," portraying a patient with Parkinson's who bonded with Harrison Ford's character. (Tommaso Boddi/WireImage)
Michael J. Fox and John Mayer attend the Third Annual Social Impact Summit at DGA Theatre July 22 in Los Angeles. (Monica Schipper/Getty Images)

Fox and Brooks received the Philanthropic Organization of the Year award at this year's Social Impact Summit. Other honorees included John Mayer, who received the Philanthropist of the Year Award, and Stephen Curry and Ayesha Curry, who received the Philanthropists of the Year Award.

title: Country singer Megan Moroney swears off dating after men 'ruined' her biggest moments
summary: Megan Moroney says some of her biggest career moments were ruined by the wrong guy, revealing why she's choosing life on tour with no distractions.
story: Country music star Megan Moroney told Fox News Digital she is not ‘emotionally available’ for a romantic relationship, putting all her energy into her music career.
Megan Moroney isn't looking for love.

The country music star said some of the biggest moments of her fast-rising career were derailed by the wrong man. Now, Moroney is choosing to take a break from dating, trading romance for life on tour, time with loved ones and, as she put it, "no man, a dog."
"It’s really nice that this is one of the first tours I’ve been on where I’m not dating anyone, so I literally have no distractions," she told Cosmopolitan.
MEGAN MORONEY STUNS IN ORANGE BIKINI DURING FRIEND'S BAHAMAS BACHELORETTE
"And that sounds really silly, but there have been a lot of big moments and fun times that have been ruined by a guy for me. It’s nice to just have a clear head.

"I’m learning what I like and what I don’t like and what my goals are," she added. "It’s been cool to be so disciplined with my routines, to see what I’m capable of when everything is going like it’s supposed to."
Megan Moroney said she's taking a break from dating, explaining that some of the biggest moments of her career were overshadowed by relationships. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images)
That doesn't mean she's sworn off dating for good — just for now.
"There is something about having a crush that’s exciting, and when my tour wraps up in October, when I’m back from Europe, I’ll maybe be on the prowl again."
Moroney said "cuffing season" might be calling her name, but life is peaceful right now.

"It’s been so nice to have my friends and family out [with me] and that not be an aspect of my life that is any sort of problem for me. … Life is peaceful. I got a dog in February. That’s what I needed all along — no man, a dog."

Moroney's decision to hit pause on dating comes after years of public speculation about her love life. The "6 Months Later" singer has been connected to a handful of high-profile country music names, including Morgan Wallen and Riley Green.
The 28-year-old rising star is known for blending witty storytelling with heartbreak-heavy lyrics.
Riley Green and Megan Moroney perform together Nov. 14, 2024. (Derek White/Getty Images for Audacy)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
While fans often try to decode the real-life inspiration behind her lyrics, Moroney said she's become more comfortable embracing the curiosity.

"In ‘Who Hurt You,’ I made it so obvious who it’s about that it was, like, you could google it, and that was the point of ‘Who Hurt You.’ In the past, I got frustrated with people," Moroney told Cosmo.

"I was trying to hint at things, and then people would be like, ‘Who is it about?’ And I was like, ‘You know what? I’m just gonna lay it out there. I might as well put his first and last name in it.’ Songwriting is fun, and it’s not meant to be taken so seriously."
WATCH: COUNTRY SINGER MEGAN MORONEY SAYS CAREER PREVENTS HER FROM FINDING ‘SOMEONE THAT I WANT TO MARRY RIGHT NOW’
Still, Moroney said she's learned not to apologize for writing from raw emotion even if listeners sometimes read more into it than she intended.
Megan Moroney revealed she's not looking for love while on tour, saying having "no distractions" has helped her stay focused on her career. (Rona Liana Ahdout for Cosmopolitan)
"It’s confidence that has grown over time, but it’s not being ashamed of how you felt. If you think it’s wrong, then OK. But this is how I felt, so here’s the song about it," Moroney said.

"I always try to explain to people that I’ve written songs about these big emotions, so they can feel huge in a song. But I could have felt that way really intensely for 10 minutes and wrote a whole song about it. And, so, in your head, you’re like, ‘Oh, this must be her whole life.’
"And it’s like, ‘Well, actually, I was just heated, and I wrote the song.’ Songs can be written from a few minutes of a feeling. So, sometimes it’s not that deep. Other times, it is that deep."

Moroney doesn't plan to shy away from documenting love, heartbreak and everything in between through her music. She said the honesty that fuels her songwriting is ultimately what keeps fans coming back.

"When I get scared of putting out a song because it’s too personal, I think about how it might help somebody, because every time I’ve done it and I’ve taken the risk, people have come up to me, and they’re like, ‘This song made me dump this guy’ and ‘This song is making me never want to go back to him,'" she recalled.
"It’s just one of those things where you have to be like, ‘F--- it. What’s the worst that could happen?’"

title: Man who beat rare cancer celebrates by canoeing 2,000 miles with his dog
summary: Frank Carter, 67, and his dog Amos completed a 2,000-mile canoe trip down the Missouri River four years after CAR T-cell therapy cleared his lymphoma.
story: Patient Laurie Adami credits the cancer treatment Car-T with saving her life on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

A 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Florida, completed a more than 2,000-mile journey down the Missouri River alongside his dog, Amos, after undergoing a groundbreaking immunotherapy treatment.
Frank Carter spent 64 days navigating the longest U.S. river in a cedar-strip canoe he built by hand, according to reports from the Moffitt Cancer Center and FOX 13 News.
The expedition began in Montana and concluded near St. Louis, Missouri, requiring the pair to camp along the riverbank while enduring severe storms, high winds and hail, FOX 13 News reported.
'FIT MOM' DID 'EVERYTHING RIGHT' — THEN A COLON CANCER DIAGNOSIS CHANGED HER LIFE

Before his diagnosis, Carter was a long-distance adventurer. According to the Moffitt Cancer Center, he spent five months hiking the Appalachian Trail in 2019 and completed an eight-week cross-country bicycle ride from San Diego to New Smyrna Beach, Florida, in 2020.
However, his physical limits were tested in a new way in 2021 after a routine 5K race.
Frank Carter, a 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Fla., paddled 2,341 miles down the Missouri River over 64 days with his golden retriever, Amos. (UCG/Universal Images Group via G)
"I was wiped out. I just wasn't recovering," Carter told FOX 13 News. "I went to my doctor, had blood tests. Long story short, in two weeks I was getting chemo."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Doctors diagnosed Carter with mantle cell lymphoma, a rare form of blood cancer that originates in white blood cells known as lymphocytes. He underwent 15 rounds of chemotherapy in Orlando, according to Moffitt Cancer Center.
Carter hand-built the cedar-strip canoe (not pictured) for the journey, and is now sharing his story to encourage other patients to remain active and hopeful. (iStock)
Although the treatment significantly reduced the cancer, follow-up exams showed lingering traces of the disease.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Carter then sought care at the Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa to undergo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, which involves extracting the patient's own immune cells, genetically altering them in a laboratory to identify cancer cells, and adding them back into the body.
Doctors treated Carter with CAR T-cell therapy, a groundbreaking immunotherapy that genetically alters a patient's own T-cells to attack cancer, leaving him cancer-free for four years. (iStock)

"We take those T-cells and genetically engineer them by putting something called a CAR into them," Dr. Michael Jain, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center, told FOX 13 News. "Now these T-cells can see the tumor and get rid of it, where before the tumor was able to hide from it."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Carter has remained cancer-free for four years after the single infusion. Throughout his recovery, he has found constant support in his dog, Amos, whom he brought home right before beginning chemotherapy.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"After my cancer diagnosis, I told myself I was going to beat this, and I really wanted a dog during the process," Carter told Moffitt's Endeavor publication. "I got Amos right before my first treatment."
